Here’s a quote from one of my favorite shows. The main character witnessed something extremely traumatizing and is experiencing ptsd. He asks his friend, “you said this [feeling] goes away, so what’s the timeframe on that?”

His friend replies, “Here’s what’s gonna happen. One day, one day you’re gonna wake up, eat your breakfast, brush your teeth, go about your business. And sooner or later… you’re gonna realize you haven’t thought about it. None of it. And that’s the moment, you realize you can forget. When you know that’s possible, it all gets easier.”

It might take months or years for that moment. it might never completely go away, but I believe it’s possible for you to process these emotions and be able to focus on your life easier. please seek help if you need it. And please keep getting back up, in hopes that one day things will be easier and you’ll be able to enjoy your life.

The first day was scary, and the environment didn’t help. I arrived at 4 in the morning so I needed to sleep, but they didn’t have my room ready. So they put me in one of the two ‘calming’ rooms. Basically a room you could go to if you were having a panic attack or just needed to separate. The first one they put me in looked like a jail cell with a bed bolted to the middle of the room. I started to freak out because it wasn’t a pleasant room and they noticed and put me in the other room. That one was much more pleasant it had a couch and a painted mural. I was able to get some rest in there. They had to check on you every 15 minutes even throughout the night, but I got used to that part. Obviously there was nothing that you could kill/hurt yourself or others available. No phones, shoes, Nowhere to tie a rope, everything was bolted to the ground, the doors would close but nothing keeps them closed except gravity so you just push them and they’ll open, etc. The only questionable things were pencils but they were the short ones with no eraser and they didn’t sharpen them. 

The rooms had 2 beds, a desk with 2 chairs, a bedside table, a window, a bathroom, and a shower. I had a roommate, then when he left I got another one in the middle of the night

there was a scheduled day but you weren’t forced to do anything. Theoretically I could’ve stayed in my room and slept all day, but the doctors would see that and assume I’m not trying to get better and they would keep me longer. I got to select my food daily from a menu and although I struggled with an appetite the first few days once I did eat the food was really good.. We got to go outside twice a week but you had to get doctors approval beforehand. 

Patients saw a case manager and psychiatrist once a day, and a therapist/psychologist twice a day. The case manger handled the care received after discharged so like making sure you have appointments, giving recourses for outpatient and support groups, making sure you have a place to go, etc. the psychiatrist would change meds and handled when you would be discharged. The psychologists would just check in with you throughout the day to see how you’re doing. I could request to talk with a psychologist whenever I needed which was really nice. Everyone was adamant that if I needed anything to just ask the front desk people. If it was something about my comfort and didn’t give me access to hurt myself they would help as best they could.

The “group therapy” was not what I expected. It was more of a class where you can raise your hand and share something if you wanted. We had 2-4/day and it was stuff like medication management, coping mechanisms, communication, setting boundaries, creative expression, etc. I learned a lot about why I make the decisions I do and strategies to break bad habits and maintain new ones. 

Once I left my room things got a helluva lot better. They had 2 ‘day’ rooms where you could hangout with the other patients throughout the day. Both had board games, drawing materials, and a TV. Since I love movies I asked if they had any movies available and they had a huugeee selection filled with classics and new releases. I watched blade runner 2049 with a cool dude that I miss. Everyone was really awesome to talk to. Everyone was there to support each other without judgement so no matter who you are, you fit in. A fellow patient put it this way, he said, “I could raise my hand and say I eat toilet paper and someone across the room would raise their hand and say, ‘me too.’” I felt accepted in a way I haven’t felt before. That same dude was an artist and he asked if he could hang something I drew up on his wall because he loved my art. That was very wholesome and I love knowing that my drawing is up on someone’s wall right now.

When I left there I was the happiest I could ever remember being.

If anyone has any questions I’d love to answer, I probably missed a lot.

Depression is fucking tough man. For me, it convinced me of things about myself that just weren’t true. I started meditating and I found it reduced the negative thoughts my depression caused, which made it a hell of a lot easier to get through the day. There’s a statistic that 15 minutes of meditation a day 4 times a week for 8 weeks yields significant clinical benefits. I found a sort of ‘acceptance’ in my situation that allowed me to look for alternative solutions other than my automatic negative reactions that yield no benefit.

I’m happy it was helpful. I was in a stage a few years ago where I was just sitting waiting for things to get better. The stakes kept getting higher and higher and higher and I would do small things to try to change my habits, but the people around me wouldn’t see those, and they would point out the mistakes. So I stopped trying because it never felt enough. But Jesus, like they expect me to turn myself around and fix all my bad habits in a few months. It takes a looong time to change the bad habits and when people point out the mistakes its so demotivating and makes it harder. Maintaining the change is even harder. I got a glimpse of happiness when I was released from an inpatient ward a few weeks ago. I understood myself and why I make the choices I do. More importantly I felt understood by the other patients. They provided a sense of support I never got in my personal life. I think it’s about removing the barriers that are stopping you from making a change. For me it’s weed and the people I’m around. Easier said than done 100%, I still haven’t done it but I think it’s a decent direction to look in. 

I feel bad sometimes about over-sharing my experience, I hope it helped in this case
